scenarios.title: Last night's deploy wrote bad data
scenarios.contextMarkdown:
Thursday's release went out at 18:00. It included a change to how invoice totals are recalculated when a line is edited — a rounding fix, three lines, reviewed and approved.

It is now **09:05 on Friday**. You open your laptop to a message from the account manager, sent 09:01:

> Delta says two invoices they sent out this morning have the wrong total. Off by a few piastres. Is that us?

You check. It is you.

The recalculation now rounds each line **before** summing instead of after. Every invoice touched since 18:00 has been rewritten with a total that can be off by a few piastres either way. A quick count: **4,127 invoice rows** across **9 clients**. The nightly export ran at 02:00.
scenarios.stakeholdersMarkdown:
- **The account manager** — asked one question and is waiting. Will pass on whatever you say, immediately.
- **Nine clients** — do not know yet. One of them has already emailed invoices to their own customers.
- **Your team lead** — not online yet. Reachable.
- **The other backend dev** — online, free, and asking if you need anything.
scenarios.constraintsMarkdown:
- You have **write access to production** for data fixes. Nobody reviews what you run there.
- Nightly backups. The most recent is from **02:00, after the bad data was already written**.
- The nightly export at 02:00 has already pushed these invoices into nine client accounting systems.
- The next scheduled release window is **Monday 18:00**. Out-of-window deploys need your team lead to approve.
- There is no audit table. Invoice rows are updated in place.

stages.label: 09:05, first fifteen minutes
stages.prompt:
You have just confirmed it is your change. Nobody outside has been told anything yet, and the account manager is waiting on a one-line answer.

What do you do in the next fifteen minutes, in order?
stages.inputHint: Order matters here. Say what you do first and what you deliberately do not do yet.
stages.modelAnswerMarkdown:
**Stop the bleeding before you fix anything.** The bug is still running: every invoice edited between now and the fix gets corrupted too. That is the first move — disable the recalculation path, take the feature down, or in the worst case take that function out of service. The number of bad rows should stop growing while you think.

**Answer the account manager immediately, in one line:** *"Yes, it's us. I know what it is, I'm on it, I'll have a full answer within the hour — please don't send anything further out until I confirm."* Two reasons. They are about to answer Delta with something, and it should be your sentence rather than their guess. And that last clause is the only thing that stops the damage spreading through people rather than code.

**Establish the blast radius before touching data.** Exactly which rows, which clients, which time window, and how far off each one is. A few piastres on 4,127 rows is not one problem — it is potentially nine client conversations, and you cannot have any of them until you can say *which* invoices.

**Check whether it escaped.** The 02:00 export already pushed these into nine accounting systems, and at least one client has emailed invoices to their own customers. That means fixing your database is no longer the whole fix, and you need to know that now rather than after you have declared it solved.

**Pull in the other dev.** They are free. One person establishes the exact affected set, the other prepares the code fix. This is a fine place to parallelize, and doing it alone just makes it slower.

**Tell your team lead.** Not for permission — so that they are not finding out from a client.

What you do **not** do in the first fifteen minutes: write an UPDATE against production. You do not yet know the correct value for every row, you have no backup that predates the corruption, and there is no audit table. An unreviewed UPDATE right now is how a bad morning becomes an unrecoverable one.
stages.revealMarkdown:
You disable the recalculation path at 09:12. The count stops at 4,127.

The good news: the bug is deterministic. Given the same lines, the correct total is recomputable exactly — you do not need the old values, you can derive them.

The bad news, in three parts. The 02:00 export sent all 4,127 into nine accounting systems. One client has **already emailed 31 of them to their own customers**. And a handful of the invoices have since been **partially paid** against the wrong total.

rubricPoints.text: Stops the bug from corrupting more rows before doing anything else
Answers the account manager immediately, and tells them to hold off sending anything further
Establishes exactly which rows, clients and time window are affected before touching data
Checks whether the bad data already left the system via the export or emailed invoices
Tells the team lead rather than letting them hear it from a client
Does not run an UPDATE against production in the first fifteen minutes
Uses the second developer instead of working alone

stages.label: Fixing it for real
stages.prompt:
The totals are recomputable exactly. But 4,127 invoices are already in nine accounting systems, 31 have been emailed to a client's own customers, and a few have been partially paid against the wrong amount.

The next release window is Monday 18:00. What do you do, and how do you make sure the repair itself does not become the second incident?
stages.inputHint: The code fix, the data fix, and how you would know the data fix worked.
stages.modelAnswerMarkdown:
**Two separate fixes, and do not conflate them.** The code fix stops it happening again. The data fix repairs what already happened. They ship at different times and carry completely different risk.

**The code fix** is a three-line revert. Ask your team lead to approve an out-of-window deploy today — this is exactly the case the exception exists for, and waiting until Monday means the feature stays disabled for three days over a rounding bug.

**The data fix is the dangerous one, and it needs to be treated like a deployment, not like a query:**

- **Snapshot first.** Copy the 4,127 affected rows, as they are now, into a scratch table. You have no backup that predates the corruption and no audit table — this snapshot is the only rollback you will have, and it costs one `SELECT INTO`.
- **Compute, then compare, then write.** Produce the corrected totals into a table beside the current ones and look at the differences before updating anything. If the fix is right, every delta should be a few piastres. Any row that moves by more than that is a row you do not understand yet, and it should stop the whole repair.
- **Run it in a transaction, in batches, with a row count you have predicted in advance.** If the count comes back 4,127, commit. If it comes back 40,000, roll back and find out why before running anything else.
- **Have the other dev read the script before it runs.** Nobody reviews production data changes here — that is a gap in the process, not a licence.

**The partially paid invoices are not a data problem, they are a decision.** An invoice paid against a wrong total is now a discrepancy with a customer, and whether you adjust, credit or leave it is a finance call, not an engineering one. Fix everything else, list those separately, and escalate them with the numbers attached. Silently changing the total on an invoice somebody already paid is worse than the original bug.

**And the export already left.** Repairing your database does not repair nine accounting systems. Find out whether the export can be re-sent for that window or whether each client has to correct their end. That is likely the longest tail of this whole incident.

**Verify by re-running the check, not by looking.** The same query that found 4,127 bad rows should return zero afterwards. That is the proof.
stages.revealMarkdown:
The revert goes out at 14:30 with your team lead's approval.

The repair script runs at 15:10. The snapshot table saves you: the first version of the fix would have touched **4,131** rows, not 4,127. Four invoices had been legitimately edited that morning, after the corruption, and your window was one hour too wide. You catch it because the number did not match, roll back, narrow it, and re-run.

Seven of the nine clients accept a re-sent export. Two have to correct their end by hand.

The 31 emailed invoices and the partially paid ones go to Delta's finance lead as a list, with a note. She thanks you for not quietly changing them.

rubricPoints.text: Separates the code fix from the data repair and treats them as different risks
Snapshots the affected rows before writing, since no backup predates the corruption
Compares computed corrections against current values before updating anything
Predicts the row count and treats a mismatch as a stop condition
Escalates the partially paid invoices as a finance decision instead of silently rewriting them
Recognises that repairing the database does not repair the nine accounting systems
Has someone else read the production script before it runs
Says how the repair will be verified — the same query returning zero

stages.label: What you say afterwards
stages.prompt:
It is 17:00. The data is repaired, the code is fixed, the exports are re-sent, and the open items are with Delta's finance lead.

Write what you send the clients — and then say, honestly, what you would change so this cannot happen the same way twice.
stages.inputHint: The client-facing note, then the change you would actually make. Not a list of best practices.
stages.modelAnswerMarkdown:
**The note, short and without hedging:**

> Yesterday evening we released a change to how invoice totals are rounded. It was wrong: totals recalculated after 18:00 on Thursday could be out by a few piastres in either direction. This affected 4,127 invoices across nine accounts, including some that reached you in this morning's export.
>
> The cause is fixed, every affected invoice has been corrected, and we have re-sent the export for the affected window. If your system has already imported the earlier file, the corrected export supersedes it.
>
> Two things we have not changed on our own: invoices that were already emailed to your customers, and a small number that were partially paid against the wrong total. Those are listed separately and we will follow your lead on each.
>
> This was our error and it should not have reached you. What we are changing is below.

**What actually changes — pick the things that would have caught this one, not a wish list:**

- **A rounding change to money had no test.** That is the real failure. Three reviewed lines went out because nobody could see what they did to a total. A handful of tests over invoice totals would have caught it in seconds, and this codebase has no tests at all — so start with the money.
- **Nothing noticed for fifteen hours.** The bug ran from 18:00 to 09:05 and it was a client that found it, not you. Even a crude check — totals that changed without a line changing — would have found it overnight.
- **Invoice rows are updated in place with no history.** The reason the morning was frightening is that you could not see what a row used to be. An audit trail on invoice totals turns the next one from an archaeology problem into a lookup.
- **The 02:00 export runs regardless.** It happily shipped 4,127 wrong invoices to nine accounting systems while everyone slept. Something between "we changed things" and "send it to the client" is missing.

**What is not the lesson:** "be more careful" and "review more thoroughly." The change *was* reviewed. A three-line rounding change that looks correct on the screen is exactly the kind that gets approved. Process discipline did not fail here — the absence of any way to see the effect did.

Write this down today, while it still stings. On Monday it will feel smaller than it was, and the thing you will actually build is whichever of these you wrote down.
stages.revealMarkdown:
You send it at 17:20.

No client asks for anything more. The one who had emailed 31 invoices sends a correction to their own customers and copies your wording almost exactly — which is why the note was worth writing carefully.

On Monday your team lead reads the last section and asks one question: *"Which one of those four do we do first?"*

That is the question you wrote it for.

rubricPoints.text: States plainly what happened and that it was your error, without hedging
Gives the specific scope — the window, the number of invoices, the accounts affected
Is explicit about what was NOT fixed unilaterally and why
Identifies the missing test on money as the actual cause of the escape
Notices that nothing detected it for fifteen hours — a client did
Proposes an audit trail, having just felt the absence of one
Rejects be-more-careful as a fix, given the change was already reviewed
Writes it down the same day rather than promising to do it later
